Nowadays, learning a foreign language is very important in the modern world. Some people think children should start to learn it in primary school, while other people believe secondary school is a better time. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, there are some reasons why starting at secondary school can be better. Firstly, older students are more mature and they can understand grammar rules more easier. For example, a twelve years old student can study by himself and use a dictionary. Secondly, young children already have many subjects to learn, like maths and their mother language, so adding another language can make them confused. Also, many primary schools do not have enough qualified teachers, so the lessons may be not good quality.

On the other hand, many people think that primary school is the best time. Young children can learn new sounds very quickly and they are not shy to speak. That is why children who learn English early usually have a better pronunciation than adults. In addition, if they start early, they will have more years to practise, and by the time they finish school they can speak fluently. Learning language can also be fun for children because teachers use songs and games.

In my opinion, I believe that it is better to start at primary school. Although older students understand grammar better, the advantage of young age is more important, especially for speaking and listening. However, the government should make sure there is enough good teachers.

In conclusion, both views have some good points. Older students can learn grammar easily, but young children learn speaking more naturally. I think children should begin a foreign language in primary school if the teaching is good.

samples.text:
There is ongoing debate about the ideal age at which children should start studying a foreign language. While some argue that secondary school is the more appropriate stage, I believe that introducing languages in primary school brings greater long-term benefits, provided it is done well.

Those who favour a later start point to the cognitive maturity of older pupils. Teenagers are able to grasp abstract grammatical concepts, use learning strategies such as keeping vocabulary notebooks, and take responsibility for their own progress. As a result, they can often cover in two or three years what younger learners take much longer to achieve. There is also a practical argument: primary timetables are already crowded with literacy and numeracy, and some educators worry that a second language might distract young children from mastering their mother tongue.

However, advocates of an early start emphasise the natural advantages of youth. Young children tend to imitate sounds effortlessly and are far less self-conscious about making mistakes, which means they are more willing to speak. A child who hears and repeats a language from the age of six or seven is likely to develop more accurate pronunciation and greater confidence than someone who begins at thirteen. Furthermore, an early start gives learners many more years of exposure, which is arguably the most important factor in achieving fluency.

In my view, the benefits of starting in primary school outweigh the drawbacks. The concern about overloading children can be addressed by keeping lessons short, playful and focused on listening and speaking, with formal grammar introduced later. The real challenge is the shortage of well-trained teachers, and this is something that governments needs to invest in.

In conclusion, although older learners have certain analytical advantages, I am convinced that children should begin learning a foreign language at primary school, as long as the teaching suits their age.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant support · logical paragraphing with a clear central idea · some less common collocations · mostly error-free sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Few educational questions generate as much debate as when a child should first encounter a foreign language. Some maintain that it should be introduced in primary school, whereas others contend that it is more sensible to wait until secondary level. Having weighed both positions, I would argue that an early start is preferable, although its success depends on how it is implemented.

The case for delaying language study rests largely on the capabilities of older learners. By the age of eleven or twelve, pupils have developed the analytical skills needed to understand how a language is structured, and they can apply techniques such as comparing its grammar with that of their first language. This allows them to make rapid, systematic progress. Moreover, deferring a second language gives younger children time to consolidate reading and writing in their mother tongue, a foundation on which all later learning depends. From this perspective, early lessons may consume valuable classroom time without producing meaningful results.

Nevertheless, there are compelling reasons to begin sooner. Young children acquire language largely through imitation and play, and they are generally uninhibited about experimenting with unfamiliar sounds. Consequently, those who start early often develop more natural pronunciation and a more intuitive feel for the language than learners who begin in adolescence, when embarrassment can hold them back. An early start also provides more years of exposure, and sustained contact over a long period is what ultimately produces confident, fluent speakers.

On balance, I find the second argument more persuasive. The concerns raised about primary-level teaching are genuine, but they relate to poor delivery rather than to the principle itself. If lessons are brief, oral and enjoyable, and are led by properly trained teachers, they complement rather than compete with literacy in the first language.

In conclusion, while older pupils learn grammar more efficiently, the advantages of early exposure are difficult to replicate later in life. Children should therefore begin a foreign language in primary school, with formal study left to secondary level.
samples.why: Fully addresses both views with well-developed, supported arguments · skilful sequencing and paragraphing · precise, flexible vocabulary · wide range of accurate complex structures · nuanced opinion sustained throughout.
